title: Cooking contest and Lester Young's room
summary: He recalls a cooking contest and visiting Lester's room with his record stack.

story.theme_name: Lester Young: the man, the sound, the Basie years
story.community_name: Remembering Lester Young: Prez the man and his sound

blocks.x: We had a cooking contest one time. It was Lester, Bumps, Lady Day, my wife Dorothy, and I think Louis was there, Louis Gonzalez, the guitar player, and Paul...

Campbell, from Chicago; or from St. Louis. And we had a cooking contest. And Bumps was gonna out-cook Lester. And you never tasted such horrible food. They were gonna what, fry steaks or something, and put gravy on them... God, it was just awful.

That was the only time I was ever in Lester's room. I went in Lester's room with him, and he had a red setter, and the red setter was so hungry that he was eatin' his own shit. Lester was too goddamn stoned all the time to feed him! The damn dog was almost dead. And he was a great, big, beautiful red setter. I forget what he called him.
But I went to his room with him... That was the night of the party with the...

...cooking contest. And I went up there with him. And I had always wanted to see his room anyway. I wanted to see exactly how he hunt his clothes, and whether he threw them in the corner or what the hell he did. So I went up with him. And he had a string, a big long string that went to the light from the bed. He'd pull that, and that would turn the light off. And beside him... He had a deal with the milkman that he'd bring a quart of milk and a half-pint of hundred-proof bourbon, Old Schenley bottle and and (?). Every morning.

And he had a vendor, as he called it -- a record player. He called it a vendor. It was a little square thing, you know, like this. And he had a stack of records about, oh, almost twelve inches high. The top record was "'Tis Autumn" by Freddie Montague. The second record was "So Rare" by Jimmy Dorsey. The third record was something by Freddie Snickleprints Prisher. And the fourth record I can't remember; it was by somebody else, Guy Lombardo or somebody. And it just kept on going... There wasn't a Count Basie record in there. There was not one record that had anything by Lester Young. I went through the whole pile.
Nothing! That's the reason why he played the

way he played. He was different. He was so different that he'd walk different, he'd act different, he talked different -- nobody could understand him unless they knew him real well. He's the first guy that told me that story about the monkey and the eagle. He told me that story and he just laughed his head off, and I just sat there and listened, and I thought, 'What's so funny about that?'
